vulnerabilities.name: Unvalidated URL-Fetching Parameter
vulnerabilities.description: A request parameter that causes the server to fetch a remote resource (url, uri, path, src, feed, avatar, image, webhook, callback, target, endpoint, proxy) accepts an arbitrary attacker-supplied host without validation against an allow-list of permitted destinations.
vulnerabilities.notes: Confirmed by supplying a URL pointing to a server-controlled listener and observing an inbound request (full SSRF), or by observing response-time/error differences between reachable and unreachable internal hosts (blind SSRF).

vulnerabilities.name: SSRF to Cloud Instance Metadata Endpoint
vulnerabilities.description: A server-side URL fetch is not restricted from reaching the cloud provider's link-local instance-metadata service, which on most clouds returns temporary IAM/service-account credentials and instance configuration without authentication.
vulnerabilities.notes: Severity depends on whether the metadata service requires a hop-limiting header (e.g. IMDSv2 token) that the vulnerable fetch would also need to forge; flag as Critical only after confirming an actual metadata response body, not just reachability.

vulnerabilities.name: Allow-List Bypass via Alternate IP Encoding
vulnerabilities.description: The destination-host validator compares the input against a denylist of textual forms (e.g. '127.0.0.1', 'localhost') but does not normalize alternate representations of the same address before comparing, such as decimal (2130706433), octal (0177.0.0.1), hexadecimal (0x7f000001), or IPv4-mapped IPv6 (::ffff:127.0.0.1).
vulnerabilities.notes: Confirmed by comparing the validator's behavior for the literal denylisted string versus each alternate encoding of the same address.

vulnerabilities.name: Allow-List Bypass via Open Redirect / HTTP Redirect Following
vulnerabilities.description: The host validator checks only the initially supplied URL, but the server-side HTTP client follows redirects, so a URL on an allow-listed domain that issues a 3xx redirect to an internal address is followed to the forbidden destination.
vulnerabilities.notes: Cross-reference open_redirect.json — any confirmed open redirect on an allow-listed domain is a direct SSRF allow-list bypass vector if the fetching client follows redirects.

vulnerabilities.name: DNS Rebinding Bypass of Allow-List (TOCTOU)
vulnerabilities.description: The validator resolves and checks the hostname's IP at validation time, but the server's HTTP client performs its own DNS resolution at fetch time; if these are separate lookups, an attacker-controlled DNS record with a very short TTL can resolve to a public IP during validation and to an internal IP during the actual fetch.
vulnerabilities.notes: Confirmed via timing: a validator/fetch pair separated by a measurable delay combined with a DNS record TTL of 0-1s is the classic signature of a rebinding-exploitable implementation.

vulnerabilities.name: SSRF via Webhook / Callback URL Configuration
vulnerabilities.description: A feature that lets the user register a webhook, callback, or notification URL (to be called by the server on an event) stores and later fetches an attacker-supplied internal address, turning a legitimate integration feature into a persistent, repeatable SSRF primitive.
vulnerabilities.notes: Higher severity than a one-shot SSRF because the fetch is typically repeated on every triggering event, giving the attacker multiple attempts and potentially a feedback channel via retry/error payloads.

vulnerabilities.name: SSRF via Server-Side Document/PDF/Screenshot Rendering
vulnerabilities.description: A feature that converts a URL or user-supplied HTML to PDF, an image, or a thumbnail renders the content in a server-side headless browser or renderer that itself fetches external resources (images, iframes, stylesheets), making any injectable URL or HTML an SSRF vector through the renderer's own network access.

vulnerabilities.name: SSRF via Remote File Import / 'Fetch from URL' Upload Feature
vulnerabilities.description: An upload or import feature offers a 'fetch from URL' option (import avatar from URL, import document from link, RSS/feed subscription) that the server fetches directly, with the same validation gaps as other URL-fetching parameters but often overlooked because the entry point is a file-upload UI rather than an obvious API parameter.

vulnerabilities.name: Blind SSRF Confirmed via Out-of-Band Interaction
vulnerabilities.description: The application fetches a server-supplied URL but returns no part of the response body to the client, so exploitation/confirmation relies on an out-of-band channel (DNS lookup or HTTP callback to an externally-controlled collaborator host) rather than response content.
vulnerabilities.notes: Confirmed purely by out-of-band DNS/HTTP interaction logs, independent of any observable difference in the HTTP response; still exploitable for internal port scanning and, via chaining, for metadata/internal-service access even without response reflection.

vulnerabilities.name: SSRF Enabling Internal Port Scanning / Service Enumeration
vulnerabilities.description: Differences in response time, status code, or error message when the fetched URL targets different internal host:port combinations allow an attacker to map which internal hosts and ports are reachable from the server, even without full response disclosure.
vulnerabilities.notes: Confirmed by diffing responses (timing, status, error text) across a range of internal host:port combinations; consistent 'connection refused'-style errors versus consistent timeouts versus a distinct 'success' response each indicate closed, filtered, and open respectively.

vulnerabilities.name: SSRF via Scheme Other Than HTTP(S) (file://, gopher://, dict://)
vulnerabilities.description: The URL-fetching component does not restrict the accepted scheme to http/https, so a non-HTTP scheme (file://, gopher://, dict://, ftp://) is accepted, enabling local file disclosure (file://) or raw protocol interaction with internal services (gopher:// for crafting arbitrary TCP payloads against services like Redis/Memcached).
vulnerabilities.notes: Confirmed by observing file content disclosure in the response (file://) or a behavioral/timing signature consistent with a raw protocol handshake (gopher/dict) against a known internal service.
